thread.title: Apple Ignores Tesla, Instead Partners With Volkswagen - Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA)

author: Anton Wahlman
title: Apple Ignores Tesla, Instead Partners With Volkswagen - Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA)
text:
New York Times broke the story of the Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) Volkswagen ( OTCPK:VLKAY ) ( OTCPK:VLKAF ) partnership for the future of the automobile industry: here.
By far the most interesting investment implication from this Apple-Volkswagen automobile alliance is the impact on Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA ) stock. If I had a dime for every time I heard, over approximately half a decade, that "if all else fails for Tesla, Apple will just buy them" - I could probably have bought the company myself. It's one of the most prevailing "last line of defense" arguments for many Tesla stock bulls.
Of course, a bull case for Tesla stock should not rely on being acquired, whether by Apple or anyone else. A sound investment case is based on a sensible earnings multiple coupled with a sound cash flow statement and balance sheet. In other words, just like Apple stock itself.
However, with Tesla's gross margins for the Model 3, and quite possibly also the stationary storage product line being negative, there's not much of an investment case for Tesla right now. It's hard to get to any level of profitability or valuation when the gross margins on the two main growth product lines are negative.
But don't worry, the bulls said - this Tesla hot potato was so attractive that it was "obvious" that Apple would have to acquire the company in the end. After all, every super-rich venture capitalist on Sand Hill Road has an Apple iPhone and at least a couple of Teslas, so how could the story end otherwise? here.
Apple didn't invest in Theranos, either.
There are multiple reasons why Apple isn't doing this. Among the broader explanations are:
It would cost Apple a lot less to replicate Tesla than to acquire it.
If Apple wanted to move faster into automotive scale, it would just buy Fiat Chrysler (NYSE: FCAU ) GM (NYSE: GM ) or Ford (NYSE: F ) and get a lot more factories for its money. Also, sooner.
Most importantly, however, is that Apple knows the warts and skeletons inside Tesla. These two companies have their headquarters a quick 18-minute drive from each other. Numerous employees have switched jobs between these two companies, in both directions, over the last six years in particular. Basically, Apple has done its due diligence here, and Apple's inaction with respect to any deal with Tesla means that they don't like what they see.
It sure isn't the absolute amount, in terms of an acquisition price, that is holding back Apple from picking up Tesla. We all know Apple's cash balance and buying power. Tesla's enterprise value may be insanely overvalued, but it's not a problem for Apple per se. The issue is something else.
Apple knows that Tesla's promise to update all of its cars (after October 2016) to Level 5 autonomy is an impossibility. This liability could, in theory, force Tesla or Tesla's future owner to buy back all Tesla cars (October 2016 onwards) because of this unfulfilled Level 5 autonomy promise: here.
This was the very first sentence, from Elon Musk, in that October 2016 rollout of Autopilot 2.0: "Basic news is that all cars exiting the factory have hardware necessary for Level 5 Autonomy so that's in terms of cameras, compute power, it's in every car we make on the order 2,000 cars a week are shipping now with Level 5 literally meaning hardware capable of full self-driving for driver-less capability."
There's no putting that mayo back into the tube. Elon promised Level 5 which he also calls "full self-driving" and "driver-less." If you bought a Tesla October 2016 onwards, that's your claim.
Actually, Tesla is pretty much the only automaker (except for Jaguar Land Rover) that has not yet announced that it has integrated Apple CarPlay, or that it will do so in next-gen cars. So if Apple and Tesla can't agree on such a relatively simple software deal, it ought to be an indication that a broader Apple-Tesla deal is totally out of the question.
So what's this deal about, that Apple seems to have struck with Volkswagen? VW isn't talking (yet), but we can draw a few conclusions from the NY Times article:
Personal chemistry Apple's management team may not trust Elon Musk, but it does trust at least one person at Volkswagen: Johann Jungwirth. He's Volkswagen's Chief Digital Officer (CDO) and he joined VW two and a half years ago after a year at Apple. Before Apple, "JJ" was a top executive at Daimler's Silicon Valley R&D facility.
A van with doors that are reliable Apple could have used the Tesla Model X minivan for its development plans, but it needed something more reliable and practical. Interestingly, according to the NY Times article referenced above, it picked Volkswagen's Transporter van.
This VW Transporter van is not sold in the U.S. Some of its main competitors from Ford, FCA (RAM), Nissan and Daimler are - but not this one. That means it will have to be approved for U.S. road use. This is not a very inexpensive process, so it's not something Apple and VW would do if this was just a matter of transporting employees between Apple's buildings scattered all over Silicon Valley. This is not some semi-outsourced bus-taxi deal. It has to be something more important than that.
Volkswagen already has an autonomous technology partner In January at CES, Volkswagen announced that it will be partnering with privately held Aurora for the development of future autonomous vehicles. Aurora was founded by Chris Urmson, who was leading the Google (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) self-driving project for years, and Sterling Anderson, who was previously Tesla's engineer for Autopilot and Model X: here. As you might imagine, VW and Apple both know what Tesla's weaknesses are, and they have no interest in getting involved with Tesla.
Tesla: No dance partner left Apple selected Volkswagen.
Google has partnered with FCA, Honda and Jaguar Land Rover. Google also probably knows as much about Tesla as Apple does.
Independent equity investment capital: Can Tesla file a registration statement and take in more equity at this point? This February 8 report from Probes Reporter suggests that there has been lots of activity between the SEC and Tesla over the last year: here. Would Tesla please detail to the investing public what is going on with this? Does any of this mean that Tesla is having difficulty convincing underwriters such as Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley to get a deal done, in terms of raising additional capital? If so, when Elon Musk says that he does not "want" to raise more capital, that may simply mean that he "can't."
I pointed out already in my February 19, 2015, article that Apple was not going to acquire Tesla, despite those rumors having been just as hot in 2014-2015 as they have been over the last year: here.
Now that, according to the NY Times, Apple has selected Volkswagen as its automotive partner, this seems to cement my verdict from a few years ago. Tesla is out of dance partners.
Disclosure: I am/we are short TSLA.
